name: Jeju Dongmun Traditional Market
label: Dongmun Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '산지천' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '산지천' (way/94897147): point nearest the subject (2454 m long); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/20998698: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dongmun Market' (363 m across).
notes: Busy old market with local food and tangerines.

text.description:
Jeju Dongmun Traditional Market is a covered market in Jeju City, and it is the largest and oldest permanent traditional market still standing on the island. It started after the end of the Japanese colonial period. A fire destroyed it in March 1954, and it was rebuilt in its current location under the same name. Today it is known for fresh seafood, street food, souvenirs and hallabong mandarins, and there is a night market of food-truck-style vendors at the back.

It photographs well because there is so much going on: bright produce, hanging signs, steaming food and a long covered frontage. The best overall picture is taken from outside, across the stream, where you can fit the market's frontage and roofline into one frame with the lit walkway in front. That also makes a good evening shot. Inside, the aisles are busy and close, so you will mostly be taking details and people-at-work shots rather than wide views.

For a second idea, Dongmun Market Gate 8 has a large entrance signboard with lanterns and stalls behind it, which suits group photos. A few footbridges on the stream north of the market are also worth a look for a different angle. Whatever you shoot, keep the lens clean, as market air can be steamy and greasy, and be polite when pointing your phone at stallholders and their produce.
text.geographic_location: In Jeju City, Jeju Province, right beside the Sanjicheon stream. The stream's park and promenade lie directly across from the market.
text.directions_text: From there it is about 3 minutes on foot to the market, heading north. The market is covered, so it is easy to spot from the opposite bank. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the market frontage across the stream. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the footbridges or when you want more of the promenade in the foreground. Inside the market, a telephoto (2x or more) helps you capture stall details without leaning over the food.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 산지천 (opposite bank of the stream, facing the market). The covered market's frontage and roofline, framed across the stream, with the lit promenade in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the market's roofline up with a horizontal line so the building sits straight. Keep some of the walkway or stream edge in the lower part of the frame to give depth. For a different picture, try Dongmun Market Gate 8 for its big entrance sign, with the lanterns and stalls behind it, which suits group portraits.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest sign or lit area to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the lights do not burn out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone still against a railing or your body for the few seconds it needs. Inside the market, use tap-to-focus on the food and a Live Photo to catch steam and movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening is the best time for the lit promenade and the night market, but it gets busy, so arrive early. The covered market also runs by day, so daytime pictures are possible.

text.access_note: The market is a working public market with an outdoor stream promenade opposite; stall and night-market times are not given here, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The covered aisles inside the market are narrow and can be crowded, so the ultra-wide lens may be awkward there.
Phone night mode usually needs the phone held steady for a few seconds.
Market air near food stalls can be steamy or greasy, so the phone lens may need a wipe.

name: Jeju National Museum
label: Jeju Natl. Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/369809426: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jeju National Museum' (343 m across).
notes: Museum of Jeju history and culture.

text.description:
Jeju National Museum is an archaeology and local history museum in Jeju. It opened in June 2001, after construction that ran from December 1992 to the end of December 2000. The displays focus on Jeju's past, including Tamna and the island's maritime culture, so it is a good place to see how Jeju's story fits together before you head out to the coast and the volcanic sights.

For photographers, the appeal is the sheer scale of the site. The outline of the museum is around 343 metres across, so there is room to step back and let the building and its surroundings fill the frame, rather than shooting one close-up of a wall. Wide, calm frames work best: clean lines, open sky and a few people for scale.

On the map, the phone icon on the map sits at the centre of the museum outline, so you are standing at the subject itself. Walk a little way along the outside of the building until you find an angle where its full width fits in the frame, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for that. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view of one section. If you go inside, remember that photography rules for galleries can differ, so look for signs or ask staff.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Jeju, South Korea. It is a large site rather than a single small building.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or railway stops for this spot, so start from where you are staying in Jeju and go by taxi or hired scooter. Ask the driver for the Jeju National Museum (국립제주박물관), or have the Korean name ready on your phone. Once you arrive, follow the paths to the phone icon on the map at the centre of the site. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole width of the building, and the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of one section. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for roof lines, entrances and architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so verticals stay straight. Keep your phone level; tilting it up makes the walls lean inwards. Include some open ground or sky around the building to show its scale, and wait for a gap in passing visitors if you want a clean shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building on screen to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a panorama for the full width, moving slowly and keeping the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright but not harsh part of the day, such as the morning or late afternoon, when light is softer and shadows are gentler. Overcast days also work well for even colour on the building.

text.access_note: The museum is a visitor attraction with its own entry arrangements, so check the official site before you go for access to the grounds and galleries.

name: Samseonghyeol
label: Samseonghyeol
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '신산공원' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '신산공원' (way/245113652): edge nearest the subject (795 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7410332: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Sacred grove around the three myth-origin holes of the Jeju people.

text.description: Samseonghyeol is a shrine site in the middle of Jeju City, tied to the island's founding legend. The story says three demigods, Go Eulna, Yang Eulna and Bu Eulna, rose from holes in the ground here about 4,300 years ago and became the first people of Tamna, the old kingdom of Jeju. Three families still bear those names and claim descent from them. The grounds are best known for the three holes framed by a large cherry tree, and that view is the busy one. For a quieter picture, try the small stream on the edge between Sinsan Park and the shrine. A Jeju photo guide describes it as a secret photo spot, and the cherry branches hang low over the water, with the shrine grounds close by. The result is a soft, layered scene of blossom, water and old trees, without the crowd around the main tree. If you want the classic views too, the holes with the big cherry tree and the red-pillared Samseongmun gate, with its signboard and tiled eaves, are both a short stroll away. Blossom season in spring is the busiest time, so go early. Keep your phone low and close to the water, and let the branches fill the top of the frame.
text.geographic_location: Samseonghyeol is in the city centre of Jeju City, in Jeju Province. The stream sits on the edge between Sinsan Park and the shrine grounds.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Jeju City and ask for Samseonghyeol or Sinsan Park (신산공원). By taxi or hired scooter is the simplest way. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the stream and branches together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the branches are overhead and you want the water and the shrine in the same frame. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out a single blossom cluster.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 신산공원 (the small stream on the edge between Sinsan Park and Samseonghyeol). Cherry branches hanging down over a small stream, with the shrine grounds nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch a little and hold the phone low so the branches arch over the top of the picture and the water fills the bottom. Turn on the gridlines and place the stream along a lower line so the frame stays balanced. For the classic view instead, the holes framed by the large cherry tree, or the Samseongmun gate, are a short walk into the shrine grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the blossom to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the pale petals keep their detail against the sky. A Live Photo can catch the branches moving over the water. Wipe the lens before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning in the spring cherry blossom season, when it is quieter. Outside blossom time the stream is calmer, but the branches will be bare or in leaf.

text.access_note: This is a historic shrine site beside a public park, so check the official site before you go for current access rules and any restrictions, such as on drones.

name: Yongyeon Pond
label: Yongyeon Pond
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '용연구름다리' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '용연구름다리' (way/75636696): middle (37 m across); moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM N538148498 (Yongyeon): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Scenic ravine pond with a suspension bridge, lit up at night.

text.description:
Yongyeon Pond is a narrow emerald channel of water squeezed between rock cliffs, running out towards the sea. The best photo here is taken from the bridge across it, known as Yongyeon Cloud Bridge, Yongyeon Suspension Bridge or 용연 출렁다리. It is about 2.2 m wide and 42 m long. Its height and its gentle wobble give pictures a dramatic downward angle, and the bridge is the main draw of the place.

Looking down over the pond towards the sea, you get the green water between the cliffs, the bridge itself and a red-roofed pavilion in the frame. The bridge is lit at night, which makes it a favourite after dark.

For a second view, the pavilion called 용연정 looks down on the tree-lined inlet, with the bridge as the subject across the water. A popular extra shot is taken from the stairs to the valley floor beside the bridge.

Expect other visitors on the bridge, and expect it to bounce underfoot. Wait for a calm moment, brace your elbows against your body and take a few frames in a row so at least one is sharp. Keep a firm grip on your phone over the drop.
text.geographic_location: Yongyeon Pond is on Jeju Island, where the pond's channel runs out towards the sea. The suspension bridge crosses the channel.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stops are nearby, so look up the bridge by name, Yongyeon Cloud Bridge (용연구름다리). Once you reach the pond, walk onto the bridge and stop at the middle of the span. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view down the channel to the sea. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the bridge, cliffs and red-roofed pavilion all in one frame, and to telephoto (2x-3x) to pick out the pavilion or the water between the rocks.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 용연구름다리 (middle of the span, looking down over the pond toward the sea). The emerald water channel running between the rock cliffs toward the ocean, with the bridge and red-roofed pavilion in the frame. For an alternative, try the pavilion (용연정), which looks down on the tree-lined inlet with the bridge across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the channel along one of the lines so it leads the eye towards the sea. Keep a corner of the red-roofed pavilion in the frame for colour. From the pavilion, use the bridge as your subject across the water. Hold the phone over the rail with both hands and wait between bounces.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly to keep the green colour and the sky detail. After dark, use night mode and brace the phone on the rail, since the bridge moves. Take a short Live Photo burst to pick the sharpest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the bridge is lit, is a favourite time. By day, go early or at a quiet moment to have fewer people on the span.

text.access_note: The bridge is open at all times and free to use.

name: Gwandeokjeong
label: Gwandeokjeong
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '관덕정' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '관덕정' (node/11338573322): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W288746175 (Gwandeokjeong): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Oldest surviving pavilion on Jeju, from 1448.

text.description: Gwandeokjeong is a traditional wooden pavilion with wide, sweeping eaves, standing on an open plaza in front of the old Jeju Mok Office complex. That pairing is what makes it work as a photo. The pavilion sits in the foreground and the long, low buildings of the office complex give it a calm, historic backdrop. The front facade, seen from the plaza, is the classic postcard angle, and it is the view most reference photos of the pavilion use. The open space in front of it gives you room to step back and fit the whole roofline into the frame. Because the pavilion is a historic building, please don't climb on its steps or platform for a picture. Spring is a lovely time to come, as cherry blossoms are reported around the pavilion. For a phone, the plaza is easy: stand square to the front, keep the eaves level, and let the complex behind fill the space above and beside the roof. If you also want a wider view, the Jeju Mok Office courtyard shows the pavilion together with the office complex. That position is worth checking on the ground, as the exact spot is not certain. Evening views of the pavilion are also described as impressive, so it is worth returning once the light drops.
text.geographic_location: Gwandeokjeong stands in front of the old Jeju Mok Office complex on Jeju.
text.directions_text: Head for the Jeju Mok Office complex; the pavilion is on the open plaza in front of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole roofline will not fit, and use 2x if you want a tighter shot of the eaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front facade, facing the open plaza in front of the pavilion). The pavilion's front facade with its wide eaves, framed against the old Jeju Mok Office complex behind it. The pavilion is just to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Face the pavilion squarely and turn on the gridlines so the eaves sit level. Keep the pavilion in the lower-middle of the frame and let the office complex fill the background. For an alternative, try a position in the Jeju Mok Office courtyard to get the pavilion and the office complex together, checking the exact spot on the ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the timber and roof tiles keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring, when cherry blossoms are out around the pavilion. Evening can also work, as the pavilion is reported to look impressive at night.

text.access_note: The pavilion is a historic site and entry rules, fees and opening times may vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole roofline into the frame if there is limited space to step back.
Gridlines help keep the eaves level in the shot.

name: Samyang Beach
label: Samyang Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Samyang Black Sand Beach' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q139717532: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Black volcanic sand beach east of the city.

text.description:
Samyang Beach is a stretch of black volcanic sand on the north coast of Jeju, in Samyang-dong, Jeju City. The dark sand against blue water is what makes it stand out, and it gives phone photos a strong, simple contrast: a dark foreground, a bright sea and a long, clear horizon. It is at its best when the sun is low and the light turns warm, and ships' lights sometimes appear on the water after dusk.

A few facts help set the scene. The beach has long been known for its black sand, which is thought to have health benefits, and a Samyang Black Sand Festival is held here each summer. In 2023 the sandy part measured about 240 m long and 64 m wide. It was given its beach designation in 2002, the same year the festival began. The beach is shrinking through coastal erosion; one 2023 study found it had lost about 30% of its size since 2018, so what you see may differ from older pictures.

For photos, walk down to the shoreline and face the sea. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines, and let the dark sand fill the lower third of the frame. The sand colour varies, and some reviewers found it greyish rather than pure black, so don't be put off if it seems less dramatic at midday. If you want a different view, Haeilli Cafe offers a sea view framed through its window, with the beach and coastline in the foreground. It is a private business, so treat it as a place to visit rather than a public viewpoint.
text.geographic_location: Samyang Beach is in Samyang-dong, on the north coast of Jeju City, Jeju Province, right on the shoreline facing the sea.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so navigate to Samyang Beach (삼양해수욕장) in Samyang-dong, Jeju City, using a map app. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is on the beach itself, so you only need to walk down to the shoreline. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the black sand, the sea and the horizon in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky at sunset, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a ship's lights or the distant peaks.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows black volcanic sand meeting the blue sea and horizon, with the sunset light and distant ship lights on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line so it stays level. Let the dark sand lead the eye towards the water, with wet sand near the waves reflecting the sky. Facing west-southwest at sunset may include distant peaks on the skyline. As an alternative, Haeilli Cafe gives a sea view framed through its window.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright sky to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours hold and the sand stays dark and rich. After sunset, try night mode and rest your phone on a wall or your raised arm to keep it steady. Live Photos can catch the movement of the waves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, around golden hour, when the low light makes the black sand and the sea look their best.

text.access_note: Check current access rules before visiting. There may be a summer swimming season, and the steam bath area has a separate fee.

name: Jeju Fortress
label: Jeju Fortress
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '관덕정' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '관덕정' (node/11338573322): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/20995065: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '제주성지' (203 m across).
notes: Remains of the old city wall of Jeju.

text.description:
Jeju Fortress was the walled town that once stood around what is now the old centre of Jeju City. A fortress existed by 1408, and the Joseon-era walls were built or expanded in 1411. They were built of local basalt and sat between two streams, the Byeongmuncheon and the Sanjicheon. The town was laid out along an east-west line, with a plaza at its heart where Gwandeokjeong Pavilion was built in 1448. The walls were pulled down after 1910, and the last demolition came in 1926. The main surviving stretch is part of the southern wall beside Ohyeondan Altar, listed as a provincial historic site in 1971. By 2015 about 170 metres of it had been restored.

For a phone photo, the pavilion is the most rewarding place to start. Its big roof and carved, painted woodwork stand out against the open ground around it, so the picture says 'old fortress town' at a glance. The wall itself is a low stone line, better as a second shot once you walk over. Keep it simple: stand in front of the pavilion on the Jejumok Gwana entrance side, switch on gridlines and keep the roof level. Then take a wider shot with some sky and open space, and a closer one of the woodwork. The pavilion is said to look especially good in the evening when it is lit.
text.geographic_location: In the old part of Jeju City on the north coast of Jeju, where the walled town once stood between the Byeongmuncheon and Sanjicheon streams. Gwandeokjeong Pavilion sits at the old plaza, and the surviving wall site lies to the south-east.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Gwandeokjeong Pavilion in the old centre of Jeju City. From there the fortress wall site is about 540 m to the south-east. Look for the stretch of stone wall beside Ohyeondan Altar. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the pavilion and the open ground around it sit together in one frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close and want the whole roof in; keep the pavilion centred so the edges don't look stretched. Try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the roof edges and woodwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 관덕정 (in front of the pavilion, on the Jejumok Gwana entrance side). The pavilion's large roof and ornate wooden structure, framed against the open ground of the old fortress town. The fortress wall site itself lies to the south-east of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the roof ridge up with a horizontal line, so the building doesn't lean. Leave a little space around the roof rather than cropping tight, so the open ground shows. Then zoom in for a second shot of the carved beams. Once you have the pavilion, head south-east to the stone wall and photograph a stretch of it, running along the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the roof detail doesn't wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against something steady, or hold your breath as it counts down.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the pavilion is lit, is the time suggested for the best look. During the day, check that the sun isn't straight behind the roof, as that leaves the woodwork in shadow.

text.access_note: Gwandeokjeong may have an entry fee or set opening times, so check the official site before you go; the wall site is outdoors but its access may also vary.

text.description: The Jeju Folklore and Natural History Museum is a stop for anyone interested in how people have lived on the island and in its landscape and wildlife. As the name suggests, it covers both Jeju's traditional culture and its natural world. For a phone photographer, the appeal is the building and its surroundings, which give you a clear record of the visit. The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum, so you can start shooting as soon as you arrive. Begin with a wide shot of the entrance or front of the building to show where you are. Then move closer for details you notice, such as signs, textures or planting. Walk a few steps to each side so you get a different angle. If there are people nearby, wait a moment for a gap, or include one person to show the scale. Check the official site before you go, as access to the grounds and the inside may be limited, and photography rules inside museums vary. Keep your phone lens clean, as a quick wipe on a soft cloth makes a visible difference to sharpness.
text.geographic_location: The museum is on Jeju island, at the position shown on the map.

Once you arrive you are already at the phone icon on the map, so there is no extra walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building and its entrance. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the whole front in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as signs or textures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It is right at the museum, so the subject is directly in front of you and you can shoot the building and its surroundings from here.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls and details keep their colour. If you take a close-up of a detail, try portrait mode to soften the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is the most reliable for exterior shots. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people, but check the opening times on the official site before you go.

name: Iho Tewoo Beach
label: Iho Tewoo Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Iho Tewoo Beach' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q139855779: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Iho Tewoo Beach is a town beach on the western edge of Jeju City, and its two horse-shaped lighthouses make it easy to photograph. They stand on the shoreline near the harbour mouth, one red and one white, and together they give a simple, friendly composition: sand in front, the lighthouses in the middle, and open sea and sky behind. The beach takes its name from the nearby village of Iho and from the teu, a traditional fishing raft once used in this area. Visitors can sometimes try riding a teu during the annual Iho Tewoo Festival, which is a good reason to bring your phone out if you happen to be here at the right time.

The airport is close, so a plane crossing the sky above the lighthouses can end up in your frame. That adds interest to a wide shot, though the noise from the planes is constant. The sand is the easiest place to stand, and you can take the classic picture without going anywhere else. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines, and leave a good amount of sky above the lighthouses. If you want a second angle, the red lighthouse and the breakwater give a view with both lighthouses together and the harbour entrance behind. Check what is open along the breakwater when you arrive, as how far you can walk may vary on the day.
text.geographic_location: On the west coast of Jeju City, in Jeju Province, next to the village of Iho and close to the airport.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed for this spot, so check local transport options from Jeju City. The beach is on the coast west of the city centre. Once there, walk onto the sand and face the harbour mouth to see both lighthouses. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both lighthouses, the sea and the sky in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched look. Use 2x or more if you want to pick out the lighthouses alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see both horse lighthouses on the shoreline, with the sea and sometimes a passing plane above. If you want a different view, the red lighthouse area shows both lighthouses with the harbour entrance behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. Put both lighthouses on one side of the frame, and leave the sea and sky on the other. Wait for a plane to cross the sky if you want it in the shot. Crouch a little to bring the sand into the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lighthouses to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. If you want a plane, take a burst or a Live Photo and choose the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to just before sunset, when the light is soft.

text.access_note: This is an open public beach, but check local signs before walking out on the breakwater, and check the official site before you go if you plan to visit during the festival.
